question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The foundation has announced that the fellowship, along with a substantial research grant, will be conferred on ___ demonstrates the most original approach to the problem.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. whoever.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The case of a compound relative pronoun (whoever / whomever) is decided by its function inside its own clause, not by the preposition that stands before the clause. The whole clause "___ demonstrates the most original approach" is the object of "on", but within that clause the pronoun is the subject of "demonstrates", so the nominative form "whoever" is required.

◦ Complete sentence: The foundation has announced that the fellowship, along with a substantial research grant, will be conferred on whoever demonstrates the most original approach to the problem.

 

• Substitution test: replace the blank with he / him — he demonstrates is right and him demonstrates is wrong, so the nominative form is needed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "whomever" — the objective form would be right only if the pronoun were the object of a verb inside its clause (e.g. conferred on whomever the panel selects). Here it is the subject of "demonstrates".

 

• Option 2: "whom" — a plain relative pronoun needs an antecedent, and none stands after the preposition "on"; it is also in the wrong (objective) case.

 

• Option 3: "who" — the case is right, but a plain "who" cannot follow the preposition without an antecedent; the indefinite (compound) form "whoever", meaning "any person who", is required.

 

NOTE

 

• Give the ticket to whomever you like (object of "like") but Give the ticket to whoever asks for it (subject of "asks"). The preposition before the clause never decides the case.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

At the annual convocation, the Vice-Chancellor singled out the two of us, Priya and ___, for special commendation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. me.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An appositive (a noun or pronoun that renames another word) takes the same case as the word it renames. "Priya and ___" renames "the two of us", and "us" is the object of the verb "singled out". So the objective case "me" is required.

◦ Complete sentence: At the annual convocation, the Vice-Chancellor singled out the two of us, Priya and me, for special commendation.

 

• If the pair were the subject, the nominative would be used: The two of us, Priya and I, were singled out. Test: drop "Priya and" — singled out … me is right, singled out … I is wrong.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "I" — the nominative case; it would be correct only if the appositive renamed a subject.

 

• Option 3: "myself" — a reflexive pronoun needs the same person as its subject in the clause. The subject here is "the Vice-Chancellor", so "myself" cannot stand in for "me".

 

• Option 4: "mine" — a possessive pronoun cannot act as the object of "singled out".

 

NOTE

 

• The case follows the word being renamed, not the word that happens to stand nearest: Two of us, Rahul and I, won (subject) but The coach praised two of us, Rahul and me (object).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

At the wedding, Rohan introduced me to a cousin of him who serves as an adviser to the Finance Ministry.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. a cousin of his.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When "of" follows a noun that is preceded by a / an / this / that / these / those / some / any / no (the double possessive), the pronoun after "of" must be a possessive pronoun — mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs — and not a personal pronoun. So it is "a cousin of his", not "a cousin of him".

◦ Corrected sentence: At the wedding, Rohan introduced me to a cousin of his who serves as an adviser to the Finance Ministry.

◦ Example: She is a colleague of mine. That habit of yours annoys everyone.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "a cousin of himself" — a reflexive pronoun is used when an action turns back on its subject; it is not used to show a family relationship.

 

• Option 2: No substitution required — incorrect, because "of him" uses the objective personal pronoun where a possessive pronoun is needed.

 

• Option 3: "a cousin of he" — the nominative "he" can never follow a preposition.

 

NOTE

 

• The same idea can be written without "of": his cousin. But whenever the pattern "a / this / that + noun + of" is used, choose the possessive pronoun: a friend of ours, these books of hers — never a friend of us or a friend of my.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Neither my immediate supervisor (a)/ nor myself had been informed (b)/ about the abrupt change (c)/ in the examination schedule. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A reflexive pronoun (myself, himself, themselves, etc.) can never be the subject of a verb. It is used only as an object (I hurt myself) or as an emphatic word beside a noun or pronoun already present (I myself saw it). Here "myself" is the subject of "had been informed", so the nominative "I" is required.

◦ Corrected sentence: Neither my immediate supervisor nor I had been informed about the abrupt change in the examination schedule.

 

• Because the verb is in the past perfect ("had been informed"), it does not change with the person of the nearer subject, so only the pronoun needs to be corrected.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Neither my immediate supervisor" properly opens the correlative pair, with "nor" to follow.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "about the abrupt change" is a proper prepositional phrase after "informed".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "in the examination schedule" is a proper prepositional phrase that completes the sense.

 

NOTE

 

• My colleague and myself attended the meeting is wrong; write My colleague and I attended the meeting. Likewise, a reflexive pronoun cannot replace "me" as an ordinary object: The letter is for myself is wrong; write The letter is for me.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The traveller, exhausted after the steep climb, placed his rucksack beside himself (a)/ and sat down (b)/ to catch his breath (c)/ before resuming the trek. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After a preposition of place (beside, near, by, behind, above, around, before, with), when the pronoun refers to the subject of the sentence, the personal pronoun (him, her, them, me) is used and not the reflexive pronoun. So the correct phrase is "placed his rucksack beside him".

◦ Corrected sentence: The traveller, exhausted after the steep climb, placed his rucksack beside him and sat down to catch his breath before resuming the trek.

 

• A reflexive pronoun is needed only when a verb or preposition turns the action back on the subject (he blamed himself). Here "beside himself" would even change the sense, because the idiom means "overcome with emotion".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "and sat down" continues the same subject with a parallel past-tense verb.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "to catch his breath" is a proper infinitive of purpose, and "his" agrees with "the traveller".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "before resuming the trek" correctly uses "before" with a gerund.

 

NOTE

 

• She had no money with her; He looked about him; They placed the child between them — personal pronouns after prepositions of place. Remember the idiom beside oneself with joy / anger (= overcome with emotion).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The cattle that belonged to the impoverished farmer were auctioned when he could no longer afford to feed it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. to feed them.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Cattle" is a plural-only noun — it does not end in -s, yet it always takes a plural verb and is referred to by a plural pronoun. The verb "were auctioned" already shows this, so the pronoun must be "them", not "it".

◦ Corrected sentence: The cattle that belonged to the impoverished farmer were auctioned when he could no longer afford to feed them.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "to feed itself" — a singular reflexive pronoun; it does not agree with the plural "cattle" and the sentence gives no reason for a reflexive.

 

• Option 3: "to feed him" — "him" would refer to the farmer, which makes the sentence absurd.

 

• Option 4: No substitution required — incorrect, because the singular "it" does not agree with the plural noun "cattle".

 

NOTE

 

• Singular-looking plural nouns: cattle, police, people, poultry, peasantry, gentry, clergy, vermin — The police have arrested the thief and taken their statements; The people raised their voices.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

Having retired after four decades of dedicated service, Anil donated all ___ he had saved to a charitable trust.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. that.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After all, everything, nothing, anything, little, much, none, only, the same, the very and after superlatives, the relative pronoun used is "that" — not "which" and not "what". "All" is the antecedent here, so the clause must begin with "that".

◦ Complete sentence: Having retired after four decades of dedicated service, Anil donated all that he had saved to a charitable trust.

 

• "What" means "that which" and already contains its own antecedent, so "all what" repeats the antecedent and is wrong.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "which" — used after a noun with a specific reference (the savings which he had made), not after "all".

 

• Option 2: "what" — it includes its own antecedent, so "all what" is redundant.

 

• Option 3: "whom" — used only for persons; savings are things.

 

NOTE

 

• All that glitters is not gold; Everything that he said was true; It is the best film that I have seen. The relative pronoun in such clauses may even be dropped, but "which" and "what" cannot replace "that".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The chairman arrived nearly an hour late for the crucial board meeting, ___ irritated the members considerably.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. which.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A relative pronoun can refer not only to a noun but to an entire preceding clause or idea. In such a sentential relative clause, set off by a comma, the pronoun used is "which". Here "which" stands for the whole fact that the chairman arrived an hour late.

◦ Complete sentence: The chairman arrived nearly an hour late for the crucial board meeting, which irritated the members considerably.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "what" — it means "that which" and needs no antecedent; it cannot follow a comma to comment on a preceding clause.

 

• Option 2: "that" — it cannot introduce a non-restrictive clause after a comma.

 

• Option 4: "who" — used only for persons; the thing being referred to is the event of the late arrival, not a person.

 

NOTE

 

• He passed the examination, which surprised everyone. Do not confuse it with the idiom What is more, … (= moreover), in which "what" is correct.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The delegation comprised twelve officials, most of ___ were visiting the country for the first time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. whom.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the pattern "quantifier + of + relative pronoun" — most of whom, some of whom, none of whom, each of whom, many of whom — the pronoun follows the preposition "of", so it takes the objective case: "whom" for persons and "which" for things.

◦ Complete sentence: The delegation comprised twelve officials, most of whom were visiting the country for the first time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "who" — the nominative case cannot follow a preposition.

 

• Option 3: "which" — used for things and animals; "officials" are persons.

 

• Option 4: "whose" — a possessive form that must be followed by a noun, and none follows here.

 

NOTE

 

• The books, several of which were rare, were auctioned; The players, all of whom were injured, withdrew. Notice that the verb agrees with the quantifier ("most … were").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Among the doctors (a)/ in this hospital, Dr. Mehta is one of those (b)/ who believes (c)/ that prevention is better than cure. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the pattern "one of those / the + plural noun + who …", the relative pronoun "who" refers to the plural word ("those") and not to "one". Hence the verb after "who" must be plural — "believe".

◦ Corrected sentence: Among the doctors in this hospital, Dr. Mehta is one of those who believe that prevention is better than cure.

 

• Contrast: when the phrase is "the only one of …", "who" refers to "one" and the verb is singular — Dr. Mehta is the only one of the doctors who believes in this method.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Among the doctors" introduces the group correctly.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "in this hospital, Dr. Mehta is one of those" sets up the plural antecedent "those" and uses the singular verb "is" for "Dr. Mehta".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "that prevention is better than cure" is a proper noun clause.

 

NOTE

 

• He is one of the few students who have cleared the test (plural antecedent) but He is the only one of the students who has cleared the test (singular antecedent).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The painting which the museum acquired it (a)/ last year is now (b)/ worth a fortune, (c)/ and everyone admires it. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A relative pronoun (which, that, whom) already stands for the noun it refers to. Repeating that noun with a personal pronoun such as "it" gives the verb a double object — this is called a redundant pronoun. The word "it" in part (a) must be dropped.

◦ Corrected sentence: The painting which the museum acquired last year is now worth a fortune, and everyone admires it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "last year is now" correctly joins the time adverb to the main verb "is".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "worth a fortune" is a proper complement, with "worth" followed directly by the noun.

 

• Part (d) is correct — here "it" is necessary, because "everyone admires it" is a fresh clause with no relative pronoun to supply the object.

 

NOTE

 

• This is the book which I bought (not which I bought it); The man whom I met yesterday (not whom I met him). Also avoid the double-subject form Those who work hard, they succeed.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

It is a matter of pride (a)/ that I, you and he (b)/ have been chosen (c)/ for the national team. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The order of persons is fixed by the meaning. In statements of praise, honour, or neutral facts, the order is second person → third person → first person: "You, he and I". The first person is placed last, out of courtesy. The order "I, you and he" is used only when the statement involves blame, guilt or a confession.

◦ Corrected sentence: It is a matter of pride that you, he and I have been chosen for the national team.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "It is a matter of pride" properly uses the anticipatory "it" for the clause that follows.

 

• Part (c) is correct — the plural auxiliary "have" agrees with a compound subject joined by "and".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "for the national team" is a proper prepositional phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember 2-3-1 for good, 1-2-3 for bad: You, he and I are eligible for the prize but I, you and he are responsible for the failure. In the plural: You, they and we (good) and We, you and they (bad).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Neither the general manager nor his assistants have completed his share of the audit before the deadline.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. have completed their share.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• With "neither … nor" (and "either … or"), both the verb and the pronoun agree with the subject nearer to them. The nearer subject is "his assistants" (plural), so the verb remains plural ("have completed") and the pronoun must be plural — "their".

◦ Corrected sentence: Neither the general manager nor his assistants have completed their share of the audit before the deadline.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "has completed their share" — the pronoun is right, but the singular verb "has" does not agree with the nearer plural subject.

 

• Option 2: "has completed his share" — both the verb and the pronoun agree with the farther subject, which violates the proximity rule.

 

• Option 3: "have completed its share" — "its" is used for things and animals; the subjects are persons.

 

NOTE

 

• If the order is reversed, everything changes: Neither his assistants nor the general manager has completed his share. The same proximity rule holds for "either … or" and "not only … but also".

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

It is not (a)/ you but I (b)/ who is responsible (c)/ for the delay. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb after "who" agrees in person and number with the antecedent of "who". In the pattern "not X but Y", the pronoun after "but" is the antecedent, so the verb agrees with it. The antecedent is "I", so the verb must be "am", not "is".

◦ Corrected sentence: It is not you but I who am responsible for the delay.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "It is not" is a proper opening of a cleft sentence.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "you but I" correctly uses the nominative case after the verb "be" in this formal pattern.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "for the delay" is a proper prepositional phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• The verb follows the person of the antecedent: It is I who am; It is you who are; It is he who is. With "not … but", agree with the pronoun that follows "but": Not you but he is to blame.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

Of the two applicants, one was rejected at the interview while ___ was offered the job on the same day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. the other.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When a definite group of two is being divided, the remaining member is referred to as "the other" — the pattern is "one … the other". The group is closed, so no third member exists.

◦ Complete sentence: Of the two applicants, one was rejected at the interview while the other was offered the job on the same day.

 

• "Another" means "one more" or "an additional one" from an open group; it would suggest a third applicant, which contradicts "the two applicants".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "another" — it points to an additional, unspecified person and is not used for the second member of a closed pair.

 

• Option 3: "other" — an adjective that needs a noun after it; it cannot stand alone as a singular pronoun.

 

• Option 4: "others" — plural, so it does not agree with the singular verb "was offered".

 

NOTE

 

• one … the other (two only); one … another … the third (three); some … others (open group); some … the others (the rest of a definite group). Also: each other / one another are separate reciprocal pronouns.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Of the three routes to the summit, (a)/ any of them is difficult for beginners, (b)/ but neither is safe in the monsoon. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Neither" (like "either" and "both") is used only when two persons or things are meant. When three or more are involved, the negative pronoun is "none" and the positive one is "any". Since there are three routes, "neither is safe" must be "none is safe".

◦ Corrected sentence: Of the three routes to the summit, any of them is difficult for beginners, but none is safe in the monsoon.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Of the three routes to the summit" correctly fixes the number at three.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "any of them" is the right pronoun for more than two, and the singular verb "is" agrees with "any".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "neither" in part (c) is wrongly used for three routes.

 

NOTE

 

• Either / neither / both → two only. Any / none / all → more than two. Neither of the two answers is correct but None of the three answers is correct.

question: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.
option_1: The two rivals never trusted each others' promises.
option_2: The librarian handed the books to Ravi and I.
option_3: Let you and I settle this matter privately.
option_4: The manager did not approve of his leaving early.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The manager did not approve of his leaving early..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only Option 4 is correct. A noun or pronoun that comes before a gerund (a verb form ending in -ing used as a noun) should be in the possessive case. After "approve of", the correct form is therefore "his leaving".

◦ Correct sentence: The manager did not approve of his leaving early.

 

• Each of the other three options contains a different pronoun error, explained below.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "each others' promises" — the reciprocal possessive is written "each other's", with the apostrophe before the "s"; "each others'" is not a valid form.

 

• Option 2: "to Ravi and I" — "to" is a preposition, so the pronoun must be in the objective case: "to Ravi and me".

 

• Option 3: "Let you and I" — after "let", every pronoun is in the objective case: "Let you and me settle this matter privately."

 

NOTE

 

• each other's / one another's — the apostrophe always comes before the s. More gerund examples: I object to his going; She insisted on my staying; We were surprised at your refusing.

question: Select the sentence that is grammatically incorrect.
option_1: It was she who lodged the complaint against them.
option_2: The house, which stands on the hill, belongs to my uncle.
option_3: He introduced me to the woman whom he said was his aunt.
option_4: Everyone except her and me was invited to the ceremony.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. He introduced me to the woman whom he said was his aunt..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In Option 3, "he said" is a parenthetical clause that merely interrupts the sentence. If it is removed, the sentence reads "the woman ___ was his aunt", so the pronoun is the subject of "was" and must be in the nominative case — "who", not "whom". The case is decided by the function of the pronoun, not by the words that come between.

◦ Corrected sentence: He introduced me to the woman who he said was his aunt.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is correct — after "It was", formal usage requires the nominative "she", and "them" is rightly objective after the preposition "against".

 

• Option 2 is correct — "which" is the right relative pronoun for a thing, and the commas correctly mark a non-restrictive clause.

 

• Option 4 is correct — "except" is a preposition here, so the objective case "her and me" is right.

 

NOTE

 

• Delete-the-parenthesis test: Whom do you think is coming? → … is coming → Who do you think is coming? But when the pronoun is an object inside the clause, "whom" stays: the woman whom he said he had met.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

He is a leader (a)/ than who (b)/ none is more (c)/ respected in the party. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Than whom" is a fixed idiomatic expression. Even though the pronoun behaves like a subject ("none is more respected"), it must take the form "whom" after "than" — never "than who".

◦ Corrected sentence: He is a leader than whom none is more respected in the party.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "He is a leader" is a proper main clause.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "none is more" correctly uses the singular verb "is" with "none", followed by the comparative "more".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "respected in the party" properly completes the comparison with a past participle.

 

NOTE

 

• The same fixed pattern appears in a scholar than whom no one is more learned and a poet than whom none is greater. Do not confuse it with ordinary comparisons such as He is taller than I (am).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

___ of the two proposals did the committee finally accept?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Which.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When the choice is from a limited, known set — here, two proposals — the interrogative pronoun used is "which", and the pattern is "which of + the / these / those + noun".

◦ Complete sentence: Which of the two proposals did the committee finally accept?

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Who" — used for persons only, and proposals are things.

 

• Option 2: "Whom" — the objective form for persons, also wrong for things.

 

• Option 3: "What" — used for an open, unlimited choice with a noun (What proposal did they accept?) and cannot be followed by "of the two".

 

NOTE

 

• Which of the two is taller? Which of you knows the answer? ("which" for a limited group) but What is your name? Who wrote this novel? (open choice).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The manager made it clear (a)/ that he found difficult (b)/ to work with (c)/ his new colleagues. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• With verbs such as find, think, consider, believe, make followed by an adjective and then an infinitive (or a clause), the formal object "it" must be placed before the adjective. "He found difficult to work" lacks this object; the correct form is "he found it difficult to work".

◦ Corrected sentence: The manager made it clear that he found it difficult to work with his new colleagues.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "made it clear" correctly uses the same anticipatory "it", which shows the pattern that part (b) lacks.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "to work with" is a proper infinitive, and the preposition "with" belongs to the verb.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "his new colleagues" completes the sentence, and "his" agrees with "the manager".

 

NOTE

 

• I consider it essential to complete the work on time; She thought it wise to stay silent; We find it hard to believe his story. Without "it" the sentence is incomplete.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Ram must have taken somebody's else umbrella by mistake from the stand.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. somebody else's umbrella.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Compound indefinite pronouns — somebody, someone, anybody, anyone, nobody, everybody + else — form the possessive by adding 's to "else", the last word of the compound, not to the first word. The correct form is "somebody else's".

◦ Corrected sentence: Ram must have taken somebody else's umbrella by mistake from the stand.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "somebody's else's umbrella" — adds the possessive marker twice, once to each word.

 

• Option 3: "somebody else umbrella" — no possessive marker is used, so the relationship between "somebody else" and "umbrella" is not shown.

 

• Option 4: No substitution required — incorrect, because the possessive 's is attached to the wrong word.

 

NOTE

 

• anyone else's opinion; nobody else's business; everybody else's problem — the 's always attaches to "else".

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

You may take whatever of the two books you prefer.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. whichever of the two books.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• For a limited choice from a known set (here, two books), the compound relative pronoun is "whichever". "Whatever" is used for an open, unlimited choice and cannot be followed by "of the two books".

◦ Corrected sentence: You may take whichever of the two books you prefer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "whoever of the two books" — "whoever" is used only for persons, and books are things.

 

• Option 3: "whomever of the two books" — the objective form for persons, also wrong for things.

 

• Option 4: No substitution required — incorrect, because "whatever" does not fit a choice between two definite items.

 

NOTE

 

• Take whichever route is shorter (limited choice) but Take whatever you need (unlimited). The same difference exists between the simple pronouns which and what.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The population of Uttar Pradesh (a)/ is larger than (b)/ those of any other state (c)/ in India. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• To avoid repeating a noun in a comparison, a demonstrative pronoun is used, and it must agree in number with the noun it replaces. The noun replaced here is the singular "population" and the state that follows "any other" is also singular, so the pronoun must be "that of", not "those of".

◦ Corrected sentence: The population of Uttar Pradesh is larger than that of any other state in India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The population of Uttar Pradesh" is a proper singular subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "is larger than" is a proper comparative structure, and "is" agrees with "population".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "in India" is a proper prepositional phrase that completes the comparison.

 

NOTE

 

• that of → singular noun; those of → plural noun. The climate of Shimla is milder than that of Delhi; The rivers of the north are longer than those of the south.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The scientist, whose research (a)/ we had funded, thanked (b)/ all of us for our support. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct as it stands. "Whose" is the correct possessive relative pronoun ("whose research" = the research of the scientist), the subject "we" is rightly nominative inside the relative clause, and "all of us" correctly uses the objective form after "of".

◦ Sentence as given: The scientist, whose research we had funded, thanked all of us for our support.

 

• "Our support" uses the possessive adjective that matches "us" — the funders — so there is no shift of person. The commas correctly enclose the non-restrictive relative clause.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "whose research" is right; "who's" (= who is / who has) would be wrong.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "we had funded" is properly formed, and the past perfect precedes the simple past "thanked".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "all of us" needs no change, since "of" takes the objective case ("all of we" would be wrong), and "for our support" is proper.

 

NOTE

 

• Do not over-correct: all of us, both of them, each of you are always objective after "of". "Whose" can also refer to things: a novel whose ending surprised everyone.
